lessons.title: My Family

phrases.english: Hello, this is my family.
How many people are in your family?
I have one brother and two sisters.
I'm the youngest in the family.
My dad's job is a doctor.
My mom is a homemaker.
My grandpa and grandma live with us.
My uncle (dad's brother) is married and has two kids.
My aunt (mom's sister) lives in Aleppo.
What's your brother's name?
Are you the oldest or the youngest?
We all love to get together on the weekend.
phrases.search_term: a family gathering at a table

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Hi Nour, how are you?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Hi Rami, I'm good, thank God.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: How's the family?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Good. I just have one brother and two sisters.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Are you the oldest or the youngest?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: I'm the middle one. My older sister is married.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.arabic: ما شاء الله. وجدك وتيتك عايشين؟
dialogue.transliteration: ma sha2 alla. w jiddek w teetek 3aayshiin?
dialogue.english: God bless. Are your grandpa and grandma alive?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.transliteration: ee, saakniin ma3na b nafs il-beet.
dialogue.english: Yes, they live with us in the same house.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.arabic: هلق مين ربى الأولاد أكتر؟ تيتك؟
dialogue.transliteration: halla2 miin rabba l-awlaad aktar? teetek?
dialogue.english: So who raised the kids more? Your grandma?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.arabic: إي، تيتا كانت دايما معنا لما ماما بتشتغل.
dialogue.transliteration: ee, teeta kaanet daayman ma3na lamma mama btishtghel.
dialogue.english: Yes, grandma was always with us when mom was working.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Do you have an uncle (paternal or maternal)?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: I have two uncles (paternal) and just one aunt (maternal).

pair.english: How many people are in your family?

response.arabic: نحنا أربعة: بابا وماما وأخوي وأنا.
response.transliteration: ni7na arba3a: baba w mama w akhuuy w ana.
response.english: We are four: dad, mom, my brother and me.
Dad's an engineer, and mom's a teacher.
Yes, I have a boy and a girl.

lessons.culture: In Damascus extended families often live close together or under one roof, and grandparents (جدو/تيتا) commonly help raise the grandchildren while the parents work. Asking after someone's family (كيف العيلة؟) is a standard part of any greeting, and skipping it can feel cold.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "كم واحد بعيلتك؟" Say your family has five people.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct Arabic but sounds like a formal register; spoken Damascene uses نحنا/احنا and بالعيلة.

exercises.tip: "نحنا" (or "احنا") is the everyday word for "we".

exercises.prompt: A friend asks: "إنت الكبير أو الصغير؟" Tell them you're the youngest.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but more literary; everyday speech is shorter.

exercises.tip: "الصغير" alone is enough in casual speech.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "_____ متجوز وعندو ولدين." English meaning: My uncle is married and has two kids.

too_formal.feedback: "الكريم" is a formal honorific rarely used in casual spoken descriptions.

exercises.tip: عمي = my paternal uncle (father's brother).

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "جدو وتيتا _____ معنا." English meaning: Grandpa and grandma live with us.

too_formal.feedback: "مقيمون" is formal/written Arabic for "residing"; spoken Damascene says ساكنين.

exercises.tip: ساكنين is the plural form of "living/residing" used for two or more people.

exercises.prompt: Say in Damascene Arabic: "I have one brother and two sisters."

too_formal.feedback: "لدي" and the dual "أختان" are Modern Standard Arabic; spoken Damascene uses عندي and أختين.

exercises.tip: عندي = "I have", used constantly in spoken Arabic instead of MSA لدي.

exercises.prompt: Say in Damascene Arabic: "My mom is a homemaker."

too_formal.feedback: This is a formal written description; spoken Damascene simply says ربة بيت / ست بيت.

exercises.tip: ربة بيت and ست بيت are both common for "housewife/homemaker".

exercises.prompt: How do you say "grandmother" in Damascene Arabic?

too_formal.feedback: جدة is correct MSA but Damascenes almost always say تيتا in daily speech.

exercises.tip: تيتا is used across Syria and much of the Levant for "grandma".

exercises.prompt: What's the Damascene Arabic word for "family"?

too_formal.feedback: أسرة is standard/formal Arabic for "family"; Damascenes say عيلة in everyday speech.

exercises.tip: عيلة is the everyday word, أسرة sounds more like news Arabic.

exercises.prompt: Arrange into the sentence: "We all love to get together on the weekend."

too_formal.item: نحن جميعا نحب أن نجتمع في عطلة نهاية الأسبوع
too_formal.feedback: This word order and vocabulary (نحن، نجتمع) is formal written Arabic; spoken Damascene uses كلنا، منحب، نتجمع.

exercises.tip: منحب + verb is how "we like to..." is said in Damascene.

exercises.prompt: Arrange into the sentence: "My aunt (mom's sister) lives in Aleppo."

too_formal.feedback: تقطن and في مدينة are formal written phrasing; spoken Damascene says بتسكن ب.

exercises.tip: بتسكن ب... is how "lives in..." is said for a woman in the present tense.

lessons.title: Where I Live

phrases.english: Where is your house?

reply.english: I live in the Mazza neighborhood

phrases.transliteration: ana saaken b Dimashq min zamaan.
phrases.english: I've lived in Damascus for a long time.
Our apartment is on the third floor.
Is there an elevator in the building?

reply.english: No, you have to go up the stairs

phrases.english: The neighborhood is quiet and close to the market.

phrases.arabic: من شو مدة إنت ساكن هون؟
phrases.transliteration: min shoo mudde enta saaken hoon?
phrases.english: How long have you been living here?
Rent is expensive these days.
Our neighbors are very nice.
Our house is close to the school and the mosque.
We're thinking of moving to a bigger house.

phrases.transliteration: shaar3na fii ma7all khoDra w forn.
phrases.english: Our street has a vegetable shop and a bakery.
When do you get back home in the evening?

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.english: Hey Sami, where do you live now?

dialogue.speaker: Sami
dialogue.arabic: ساكن بحي ركن الدين، بشقة صغيرة.
dialogue.transliteration: saaken b7ay Rukn id-Diin, b sha22a sghiire.
dialogue.english: I live in the Rukn id-Din neighborhood, in a small apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.english: Okay, which floor?

dialogue.speaker: Sami
dialogue.arabic: بالطابق التاني. ما في مصعد بس مو مشكلة.
dialogue.transliteration: bit-Taabe2 it-taani. ma fii mas3ad bas mu mishkle.
dialogue.english: On the second floor. There's no elevator but it's not a problem.

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.arabic: وقديش الأجرة، إذا ما في مانع؟
dialogue.transliteration: w 2addeesh il-ujra, iza ma fii maane3?
dialogue.english: And how much is the rent, if you don't mind?

dialogue.speaker: Sami
dialogue.english: About five hundred dollars a month.

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.english: A bit expensive but the neighborhood is good.

dialogue.speaker: Sami
dialogue.arabic: إي، هادي وفيها كل شي قريب.
dialogue.transliteration: ee, haadi w fiiha kell shi 2ariib.
dialogue.english: Yeah, it's quiet and everything is close.

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.english: And how are your neighbors?

dialogue.speaker: Sami
dialogue.arabic: لطاف كتير، بيساعدوني لما بحتاج شي.
dialogue.transliteration: leTaaf ktiir, byse3duuni lamma ba7taaj shi.
dialogue.english: Very nice, they help me when I need something.

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.arabic: طيب يعطيك العافية، خليك مبسوط بالبيت الجديد.
dialogue.transliteration: Tayyeb ya3Tiik il-3aafye, khalliik mabsooT bil-beet ij-jdiid.
dialogue.english: Well, take care, stay happy in the new place.

dialogue.speaker: Sami
dialogue.english: Thanks (God keep you well), come visit me sometime.

response.english: I live in the Qassaa neighborhood.

pair.english: Which floor do you live on?

lessons.culture: Damascenes usually describe where they live by حي (neighborhood) rather than a formal address, and naming the neighborhood alone is enough for someone else to picture it. Talking about rent (أجرة) and building floors is normal small talk, and asking a neighbor for help is common and expected in most حارات (old quarters).

exercises.prompt: Someone asks "وين بيتك؟". Say you live in the Mazza neighborhood.

too_formal.feedback: "أسكن في" is written/formal Arabic; spoken Damascene says ساكن ب (dropping the extra في).

exercises.tip: ساكن/ساكنة ب... is how you state where you live.

exercises.prompt: A friend asks "من شو مدة إنت ساكن هون؟". Say about ten years.

too_formal.feedback: "منذ" and "سنوات" are formal written Arabic; spoken Damascene says من and سنين.

exercises.tip: من + a length of time is how "for [duration]" is said.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "بيتنا بالطابق _____." English meaning: Our apartment is on the third floor.

too_formal.feedback: "الثالث" is the written/MSA form; spoken Damascene says التالت.

exercises.tip: التالت = third, following the Damascene number pattern (تاني، تالت، رابع...).

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "جيراننا _____ كتير." English meaning: Our neighbors are very nice.

too_formal.feedback: لطفاء is the plural form used in formal written Arabic; spoken Damascene says لطاف.

exercises.tip: لطاف is the everyday plural of "nice/kind" for people.

exercises.prompt: Say: "The neighborhood is quiet and close to the market."

too_formal.feedback: هادئ is the MSA spelling/pronunciation; spoken Damascene drops the hamza and says هادي.

exercises.tip: هادي (quiet) is used for places, هادئ is the more formal spelling.

exercises.prompt: Say: "We're thinking of moving to a bigger house."

too_formal.item: نحن نفكر بالانتقال إلى منزل أكبر
too_formal.feedback: نحن، بالانتقال، إلى، ومنزل are all formal written choices; spoken Damascene uses عم نفكر، عبيت.

exercises.tip: عم + present tense verb is the ongoing "-ing" form in Damascene.

exercises.prompt: What's the Damascene word for "neighborhood"?

too_formal.feedback: This is a formal descriptive term ("residential area"); everyday speech just says حي or حارة.

exercises.tip: حي (or حارة for an old quarter) is the everyday word for neighborhood.

exercises.prompt: What's the Damascene word for "elevator"?

too_formal.feedback: "كهربائي" (electric) is an unnecessary formal addition; spoken Damascene just says مصعد.

exercises.tip: مصعد is used the same in speech and writing, unlike many other words.

exercises.prompt: Arrange into the sentence: "Our house is close to the school and the mosque."

too_formal.feedback: منزل and المسجد are the more formal written words; spoken Damascene says بيت and الجامع.

exercises.tip: الجامع is the everyday word for mosque; المسجد is more formal/written.

exercises.prompt: Arrange into the sentence: "Rent is expensive these days."

too_formal.item: إيجار المنزل مرتفع في هذه الأيام
too_formal.feedback: إيجار، مرتفع، في هذه الأيام are all formal written choices; spoken Damascene uses أجرة، غالية، هالأيام.

exercises.tip: هالأيام ("these days") is a fused everyday form of هذه الأيام.

lessons.title: Rooms and Things at Home

phrases.english: Come, let me show you the house.
phrases.search_term: a person giving a house tour

phrases.english: This is the living room, here we receive guests.

phrases.arabic: المطبخ عالشمال، وفيه كل شي جديد.
phrases.transliteration: il-maTbakh 3ash-shmaal, w fii kell shi jdiid.
phrases.english: The kitchen is on the left, everything in it is new.
Where's the bathroom, please?

phrases.arabic: هاي غرفة نومي، صغيرة بس مرتبة.
phrases.transliteration: hay ghurfet noomi, sghiire bas mrattabe.
phrases.english: This is my bedroom, small but tidy.

phrases.transliteration: fii takht w khazaane w maktab bil-ghurfe.
phrases.english: There's a bed, a closet and a desk in the room.

phrases.arabic: الطاولة والكراسي جداد، اشتريناهن الشهر الماضي.
phrases.transliteration: iT-Taawle w il-karaasi jdaad, ishtareenaahen ish-shahr il-maaDi.
phrases.english: The table and chairs are new, we bought them last month.

phrases.arabic: الثلاجة عم تعمل صوت، لازم نصلحها.
phrases.english: The fridge is making noise, we need to fix it.
The window in my room looks out onto the garden.
Can I turn on the AC? The weather is hot.
The main door is always locked at night.
I really liked the house, tidy and nice.

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: Hi, please come in.

dialogue.speaker: Huda
dialogue.english: Thanks, your house is really nice.

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: Come, let me show you the living room here.

dialogue.speaker: Huda
dialogue.transliteration: ma sha2 alla, waase3 w naDiif.
dialogue.english: Wow, spacious and clean.

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.arabic: والمطبخ من هون، لسا رتبتو الأسبوع الماضي.
dialogue.transliteration: w il-maTbakh min hoon, lissa rattabto il-usboo3 il-maaDi.
dialogue.english: And the kitchen is this way, I just organized it last week.

dialogue.speaker: Huda
dialogue.english: Really nice, is the fridge new?

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: Yes, we just bought it two months ago.

dialogue.speaker: Huda
dialogue.english: Where's the bathroom, can I wash my hands?

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: Straight ahead and then to the right.

dialogue.speaker: Huda
dialogue.transliteration: yislamo. w shoo hay il-ghurfe iS-sghiire?
dialogue.english: Thanks. And what's this small room?

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: This is the kids' bedroom.

dialogue.speaker: Huda
dialogue.arabic: مرتبة كتير ما شاء الله. تسلم إيديكي عالبيت الحلو.
dialogue.transliteration: mrattabe ktiir ma sha2 alla. tislam iideeki 3al-beet il-7ilu.
dialogue.english: Very tidy, God bless. Well done on the beautiful house.

response.transliteration: takht w khazaane w Taawle sghiire.
response.english: A bed, a closet, and a small table.
Yes, we renovated it this year.

pair.english: Can you open the window? It's hot.

lessons.culture: A Damascene home visit almost always starts with a short tour, and a guest is expected to praise the house (بيتك حلو / ما شاء الله) as they're shown around. "ما شاء الله" is said when admiring something to ward off envy, and refusing tea or coffee offered during the visit is considered impolite.

exercises.prompt: A guest asks "وين الحمام لو سمحت؟". Tell them straight ahead, on the right.

too_formal.item: على طول الممر ثم إلى اليمين
too_formal.feedback: This is an overly formal, written-style direction; spoken Damascene keeps it short: عالطول، عاليمين.

exercises.tip: عالطول means "straight ahead" in directions.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks "فيني افتح المكيف؟". Say yes of course, go ahead.

too_formal.feedback: نعم and بالطبع are formal written Arabic; spoken Damascene says إي and أكيد/طبعا.

exercises.tip: إي (or ايه) is the everyday spoken "yes", not just نعم.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "المطبخ عالشمال، وفيه كل شي _____." English meaning: The kitchen is on the left, everything in it is new.

too_formal.feedback: حديث is a formal written word for "new/modern"; spoken Damascene just says جديد.

exercises.tip: جديد is the everyday word for "new".

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "الشباك بغرفتي _____ عالحديقة." English meaning: The window in my room looks out onto the garden.

too_formal.feedback: The MSA-marked verb form يُطِلّ with its vowel marks is written Arabic; spoken Damascene says مطل/مطلة as a simple adjective.

exercises.tip: مطل ع... is how "overlooking/facing" is said.

exercises.prompt: Say: "This is my bedroom, small but tidy."
exercises.answer: هاي غرفة نومي، صغيرة بس مرتبة
accepted: هاي غرفة نومي، صغيرة بس مرتبة
هاي غرفت نومي صغيرة بس مرتبة

too_formal.item: هذه غرفة نومي، صغيرة لكنها مرتبة
too_formal.feedback: هذه and لكنها are formal written Arabic; spoken Damascene uses هاي and بس.

exercises.tip: بس is the everyday word for "but", used constantly instead of لكن.

exercises.prompt: Say: "The fridge is making noise, we need to fix it."
exercises.answer: الثلاجة عم تعمل صوت، لازم نصلحها
accepted: الثلاجة عم تعمل صوت، لازم نصلحها
الثلاجة عم تعمل صوت لازم نصلحا

too_formal.feedback: تصدر ضوضاء and يجب are formal written Arabic; spoken Damascene says عم تعمل صوت and لازم.

exercises.tip: لازم is the everyday word for "must/need to".

exercises.prompt: What's the Damascene word for "living room"?

too_formal.feedback: "غرفة الجلوس" is a descriptive formal term; spoken Damascene just says صالون.

exercises.tip: صالون is the room where guests are received.

exercises.prompt: What's the Damascene word for "closet/wardrobe"?

too_formal.feedback: This literal descriptive phrase ("clothes cabinet") is more explanatory than what's actually said; spoken Damascene just says خزانة.

exercises.tip: خزانة covers any closet or cabinet, for clothes or otherwise.

exercises.prompt: Arrange into the sentence: "There's a bed, a closet and a desk in the room."

too_formal.item: يوجد سرير وخزانة ومكتب في الغرفة
too_formal.feedback: يوجد and سرير and في الغرفة are all formal written choices; spoken Damascene says في، تخت، بالغرفة.

exercises.tip: في at the start of a sentence means "there is/are" in spoken Arabic.

exercises.prompt: Arrange into the sentence: "The main door is always locked at night."

too_formal.item: الباب الرئيسي مغلق دائما في الليل
too_formal.feedback: مغلق، دائما، في الليل are the formal written choices; spoken Damascene uses مقفل، دايما، بالليل.

exercises.tip: مقفل (locked) and مسكر (closed) are both common; مغلق is the more formal/written word.

lessons.title: Talking About Relatives

phrases.english: What happened with your (maternal) uncle?
Is he married?
My older sister has been married for two years.
She has a little boy who's a year old.
My paternal cousin lives abroad.
My maternal cousin is studying medicine.

phrases.arabic: جدي توفي من كم سنة، الله يرحمو.
phrases.transliteration: jiddi tawaffa min kam sane, alla yer7amo.
phrases.english: My grandfather passed away a few years ago, may God have mercy on him.

phrases.arabic: تيتا هلق عايشة لحالها بس منزورها كل أسبوع.
phrases.transliteration: teeta halla2 3aayshe la7aala bas minzoorha kell isboo3.
phrases.english: Grandma lives alone now but we visit her every week.
My paternal and maternal uncles are arguing about the inheritance.

phrases.arabic: كل العيلة منتجمع بالعيد عند جدي.
phrases.english: The whole family gets together at grandpa's for the holiday.

phrases.arabic: من زمان ما شفت ابن خالتي.
phrases.transliteration: min zamaan ma shefet ebn khaalti.
phrases.english: I haven't seen my maternal cousin in a long time.

phrases.arabic: لازم نزور عمتي، صارلنا كتير ما رحنا.
phrases.transliteration: laazem nzuur 3ammti, Saarlna ktiir ma re7na.
phrases.english: We should visit my paternal aunt, it's been a while since we went.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Hi Walid, I saw you at the wedding yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Waleed
dialogue.english: Yeah, it was my maternal cousin's wedding.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Congrats to him. What's the bride's name?

dialogue.speaker: Waleed
dialogue.arabic: اسمها رنا، من بنات عمي بالحقيقة.
dialogue.english: Her name is Rana, she's actually one of my paternal cousins.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: So he married a relative of his?

dialogue.speaker: Waleed
dialogue.arabic: إي، هون كتير مبين هيك شي عادي.
dialogue.transliteration: ee, hoon ktiir mbayyen heek shi 3aadi.
dialogue.english: Yeah, here that's very much a normal thing.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: And did your grandfather attend the wedding?

dialogue.speaker: Waleed
dialogue.arabic: لأ، جدي توفي من سنتين الله يرحمو.
dialogue.transliteration: la2, jiddi tawaffa min sinteen alla yer7amo.
dialogue.english: No, my grandfather passed away two years ago, may God rest him.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: God rest him. And your grandma?

dialogue.speaker: Waleed
dialogue.english: Grandma was there, very happy.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: يسلم قلبها. طيب سلملي عليها وع العيلة كلها.
dialogue.english: Bless her heart. Well, say hi to her and the whole family for me.

dialogue.speaker: Waleed
dialogue.english: Thanks, I'll definitely say hi.

response.english: He's fine, just busy with work.
Yes, a boy and a girl.

response.arabic: لأ، الله يرحمو، توفي من زمان.
response.transliteration: la2, alla yer7amo, tawaffa min zamaan.
response.english: No, God rest him, he passed away a long time ago.

pair.english: Where does your paternal cousin live?

lessons.culture: Marriage between cousins (especially ابن/بنت العم) is still common and unremarkable in Damascus, so it comes up naturally in conversation without being treated as unusual. When someone mentions a relative who has died, the listener always answers with الله يرحمو / يرحمها (God have mercy on him/her), and skipping this is considered rude.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks "هو متجوز؟" about your cousin. Say no, he's still single.

too_formal.feedback: "لا يزال" is formal written Arabic for "still"; spoken Damascene uses لسا.

exercises.tip: لسا means "still/not yet" and is used constantly in speech.

exercises.prompt: A friend mentions their grandfather passed away. Respond with "God have mercy on him."

too_formal.feedback: This longer, more formal phrase is used in writing or religious speech; spoken Damascene simply says الله يرحمو.

exercises.tip: الله يرحمو/يرحمها is said automatically whenever someone who died is mentioned.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "أختي الكبيرة _____ من سنتين." English meaning: My older sister has been married for two years.

too_formal.feedback: متزوجة with the ت-ز pattern is the MSA spelling; spoken Damascene shifts it to متجوزة.

exercises.tip: Damascene often turns MSA تزوج (marry) into تجوز, so "married" becomes متجوز/متجوزة.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "بنت خالتي عم _____ طب." English meaning: My maternal cousin is studying medicine.

too_formal.feedback: This formal descriptive phrase ("receiving her education in") is far more elaborate than needed; spoken Damascene just says عم تدرس.

exercises.tip: عم + present tense verb makes the ongoing "is studying" form.

exercises.prompt: Say: "My paternal cousin lives abroad."

too_formal.feedback: يعيش في الخارج is the formal written phrase for "lives abroad"; spoken Damascene says عايش برا البلد.

exercises.tip: برا البلد is the everyday way to say "abroad/outside the country".

exercises.prompt: Say: "The whole family gets together at grandpa's for the holiday."
exercises.answer: كل العيلة منتجمع بالعيد عند جدي
accepted: كل العيلة منتجمع بالعيد عند جدي
كل العيلة بتتجمع بالعيد عند جدي

too_formal.item: تجتمع العائلة بأكملها في العيد عند جدي
too_formal.feedback: تجتمع and بأكملها are formal written choices; spoken Damascene uses منتجمع and كل العيلة.

exercises.tip: عند جدي means "at grandpa's place", using عند for location the way "chez" works in French.

exercises.prompt: What's the Damascene word for "maternal uncle" (mom's brother)?

too_formal.feedback: This explanatory phrase ("mother's brother") is not how it's actually said; spoken Damascene just uses the single word خال.

exercises.tip: خال is mom's brother; عم is dad's brother, a distinction Arabic keeps that English doesn't.

exercises.prompt: What's the Damascene word for "still/not yet" as in "still single"?

too_formal.feedback: "لا يزال" is the formal written equivalent of "still"; spoken Damascene uses لسا constantly.

exercises.tip: لسا can mean both "still" and "not yet" depending on context.

exercises.prompt: Arrange into the sentence: "We should visit my paternal aunt, it's been a while since we went."
exercises.answer: لازم نزور عمتي، صارلنا كتير ما رحنا
accepted: لازم نزور عمتي، صارلنا كتير ما رحنا

too_formal.item: يجب أن نزور عمتي فقد مضى وقت طويل منذ ذهبنا
too_formal.feedback: يجب أن، فقد، منذ are all formal written connectors; spoken Damascene uses لازم and صارلنا... ما.

exercises.tip: صارلنا + time + ما + verb is the spoken pattern for "it's been [time] since we...".

exercises.prompt: Arrange into the sentence: "My paternal and maternal uncles are arguing about the inheritance."

too_formal.feedback: يتجادلان (dual form) and حول are formal written Arabic; spoken Damascene uses the plural يتخانقوا and عم for ongoing action.

exercises.tip: يتخانقوا (bicker/argue) is a common everyday verb, stronger and more casual than يتجادلوا.

challenge.title: Tell Me About Your Family and Home
challenge.instructions: Have a conversation of at least 10 lines about your family and your home. It must include how many people are in your family, at least two named relatives (with their relation, like أخ or خالة), whether someone is married or single, a description of your house or apartment (rooms and floor), and one line about the neighborhood or rent. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 2 and include both a masculine-address and a feminine-address question.
required_elements: A statement of how many people are in the family, like كم واحد بعيلتك؟ or نحنا... بالعيلة.
At least two named relatives with their relation, such as أخي، أختي، عمي، خالتي، جدي or تيتا.
A married/single statement using متجوز، متجوزة، or أعزب.
A description of the house using بيت، شقة، or a room word like صالون، مطبخ، or غرفة نوم.
Which floor the home is on, using طابق.
A comment on the neighborhood or rent using حي، هادي، or أجرة.
A masculine-address question using إنت, like إنت وين ساكن؟
A feminine-address question using إنتي, like إنتي وين ساكنة؟

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Hi Hiba, how are you?

dialogue.speaker: Hiba
dialogue.english: Hi Rami, good, thank God.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: How many people are in your family?

dialogue.speaker: Hiba
dialogue.arabic: نحنا خمسة: بابا وماما وأخوي وأختي وأنا.
dialogue.transliteration: ni7na khamse: baba w mama w akhuuy w ekhti w ana.
dialogue.english: We're five: dad, mom, my brother, my sister and me.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Are you the oldest or the youngest?

dialogue.speaker: Hiba
dialogue.english: I'm the middle one. My older sister is married.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Okay, where do you live now?

dialogue.speaker: Hiba
dialogue.arabic: ساكنة بحي المهاجرين، بشقة بالطابق التاني.
dialogue.transliteration: saakne b7ay il-Muhaajriin, b sha22a bit-Taabe2 it-taani.
dialogue.english: I live in the Muhajireen neighborhood, in an apartment on the second floor.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.transliteration: w enta ya Kariim, ween beetak?
dialogue.english: And you Kareem, where's your house?

dialogue.speaker: Kareem
dialogue.arabic: بيتي بحي القصاع، عندي صالون ومطبخ وغرفتين نوم.
dialogue.transliteration: beeti b7ay il-2aSSaa3, 3indi Saaloon w maTbakh w ghurfteen noom.

dialogue.speaker: Hiba
